summary: Rachel Lee Nabors opens with her credentials across web standards: Mozilla Firefox DevTools, the W3C Web Animations API, Microsoft Edge as PM, and the React docs. She is now principal developer experience engineer at Arize, consults on web/AI/UI, writes 'The Agentic Web' newsletter, and built ASA, an MCP app for Twitter/BlueSky. Her motivating project is rachelagreat.com, a 2006-era comic archive with 400,000 weekly readers now suffering 404s and broken CDNs. She wants to future-proof it for humans in browsers, humans in agents, and agents in browsers. She contrasts STDIO (local process, CLI config) with HTTP (web service, POST, serverless-friendly) MCP transports, and demos comic-site tools returning structured JSON plus a markdown transcript tool. She laments MCP resources being loosely defined and under-implemented, arguing they should let harnesses pre-prime context rather than forcing agents to fetch docs via tools. The core argument against chat: it is the CLI of agentic software—a 'starfish' landing page that offloads discovery to users. MCP apps solve this by bundling HTML/CSS/JS into single files rendered in iframes inside agent interfaces. She demos 'get page,' which returns a full comic reader app inside Claude with navigation, commentary, comments, and a transcript mode—all matching the original website. MCP apps are sandboxed islands: no local storage, no network access, external resources need CSP configuration, links require host permissions, and server interactions use a 'call server' tool. Tools not meant for display should set visibility to 'app.' She then introduces WebMCP, which makes every HTML page a mini MCP tools server for browser agents—likening it to JavaScript vs Java (inspired by, not compliant with, MCP). WebMCP offers a declarative model (add tool name/description attributes to existing forms) and an imperative model (navigator.modelContext.registerTools with callbacks). She demos it via an MCP debugging extension, showing navigation and transcript retrieval, plus a Web Speech API text-to-speech comic reader. She closes: the web isn't dead—it's evolving, and CSS and JavaScript are the language of interactive agent experiences.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.
temporalContext: Transcript claims reflect the publication date; linked external context was checked at the run's research date.
takeaways: Chat is to agentic UX what the CLI was to desktop computing—developers love it, but 'starfish' chatbox landing pages offload too much discovery to users.
MCP apps bundle HTML, CSS, and JavaScript into a single file rendered in an iframe inside agent interfaces, turning tool responses into real interactive surfaces.

MCP apps are sandboxed islands: no local storage, no direct network access, external resources require CSP configuration, links require host permissions, and server interactions go through a 'call server' tool.
Tools not meant to be displayed as JSON should set visibility to 'app' so the model doesn't try to render their output as text.
WebMCP makes every HTML page a mini MCP tools server for browser agents, avoiding screenshot parsing and DOM traversal that burn tokens.
WebMCP is to MCP as JavaScript is to Java—inspired by the spec but not one-to-one compliant; specs may diverge.
WebMCP's declarative model adds tool name and description attributes to existing forms; the imperative model uses navigator.modelContext.registerTools with execution callbacks.
Native browser APIs—Web Speech, Animation, Audio, Canvas, WASM, CSS—are zero-dependency resources already available for building agent interactive experiences.
STDIO MCP servers run as local processes; HTTP MCP servers fit serverless/edge deployments and are far easier for end users to add in Claude.
MCP resources remain under-implemented across clients, preventing context pre-priming that would be more efficient than fetching docs via tools.

sections.title: Introduction and Speaker Background
sections.summary: Rachel Lee Nabors introduces herself and her work on web standards (Mozilla, W3C, Microsoft Edge, React docs), her current role at Arize, her newsletter 'The Agentic Web,' and her ASA MCP app for Twitter/BlueSky. She frames the browser as an infinite canvas.

sections.title: Motivations for Future-Proofing the Web Comic Site
sections.summary: Her 2006-era web comic archive (rachelagreat.com, 400,000 weekly readers on iVillage) is degrading with 404s and broken CDNs. She wants to future-proof it for three client types: humans in browsers, humans in agents, and agents in browsers.

sections.title: Roadmap: MCP, Apps, and WebMCP
sections.summary: Outlines three areas: MCP tools and transports, MCP apps (with footguns), and WebMCP. Polls the audience on hosting MCP servers, building MCP apps, and trying WebMCP.

sections.title: Understanding Transports: STDIO vs HTTP
sections.summary: Contrasts STDIO (local process spawned by client, command-line JSON config, alive throughout session) with HTTP (web service at an endpoint, POST requests, serverless-friendly). Demos adding an HTTP MCP server in Claude by pasting a URL.

sections.title: Defining MCP Tools
sections.summary: Shows her comic-site tools: list comics, list storylines, list characters, search comics by transcript, search by character, and get transcripts (returns markdown). All return structured JSON except the transcript tool.

sections.title: The Role of MCP Resources
sections.summary: Laments MCP resources are loosely defined and loosely implemented, with no client surfacing them in the UI. Argues resources would let harnesses pre-prime context rather than forcing agents to fetch docs via tools.

sections.title: The Case Against Chat-Only UI
sections.summary: Argues chat is the CLI of agentic software—a 'starfish' chatbox landing page that offloads discovery to users who must already know what the system can do. likens it to doing taxes via text adventure commands. Introduces MCP apps as the alternative: bundling HTML, CSS, and JavaScript into single files that agent interfaces render interactively.

sections.title: MCP Apps: Building Interactive Agent Interfaces
sections.summary: Demos 'get page,' an MCP tool that returns a full comic-reader app inside Claude with navigation, commentary, comments, and transcript mode matching the original website. Explains the tool definition with input schema and a meta UI attribute pointing at a URL. Details MCP app constraints: single HTML files with base64-embedded resources, sandboxed iframe, no local storage, no network access, external resources require CSP, links require host permissions, server interactions via call-server tool, and tools not for display should use visibility: app. Recommends building with an existing design system and tools like V single file.

sections.title: Introducing WebMCP: Agents in the Browser
sections.summary: Introduces WebMCP as a way for browser agents to call page functions directly without screenshot parsing or DOM traversal. Clarifies WebMCP is to MCP as JavaScript is to Java—inspired by but not compliant with the spec. Presents two flavors: declarative (add tool name and description attributes to forms) and imperative (navigator.modelContext.registerTools with callbacks for API calls, workflows, data transformation).

sections.title: WebMCP Demo with the Debugging Extension
sections.summary: Demos WebMCP using an MCP debugging extension that imitates an in-browser agent. Shows reading a comic transcript and navigating to the next page via model-called functions. Notes the standards are still being debated and points to an interview with WebMCP's creator (originally built at Amazon for auth issues) as the best starting resource.

sections.title: Leveraging Native Browser APIs
sections.summary: Demos a Web Speech API text-to-speech comic reader narrating panel descriptions with zero dependencies. Lists native browser APIs available for agent experiences: Web Speech, Animation, Audio, Canvas, WASM, CSS. Closes that the web isn't dead—it's evolving, and CSS and JavaScript are the language of interactive agent experiences on the infinite canvas.

demonstrations: Adding an HTTP MCP server in Claude by entering a name and a URL ending in /mcp, then granting always-allow permissions.
Calling comic-site MCP tools: list comics, list storylines, list characters, search by transcript, search by character, and get transcripts (markdown).
Demoing 'get page' MCP tool that returns a full comic-reader app inside Claude with navigation, commentary, comments, and transcript mode—matching the original website.
Demoing WebMCP via an MCP debugging extension: reading a comic transcript and navigating to the next page through agent function calls.
Demoing a Web Speech API text-to-speech version of the comic reader, narrating panel descriptions with zero dependencies.
limitations: MCP resources spec is loosely defined and loosely implemented; no client currently surfaces resources in the UI.
MCP apps are sandboxed islands with no local storage, no direct network access, and require CSP configuration for external resources.
WebMCP is not one-to-one compliant with the MCP spec; standards bodies are still debating it and it is not fully supported.
Browser agents still struggle with website navigation, relying on compute-intensive screenshot parsing or DOM traversal that burns tokens.
Web Speech API output 'sounds terrible' out of the box, though better with services like ElevenLabs.
quantitativeClaims: Her web comic on the iVillage network had 400,000 weekly readers around 2006.
